When I started this homesteading column I was not sure I would find enough to write about. Next I was concerned that I wasn't an adequate authority on some of the topics to which I hoped to give treatment, but this concern turned out to be unfounded.

 

A couple of weeks went by, and I knew what I most wanted to write about. I wanted to give advice to guys who were just getting started at homesteading, or who were completely hobbyists and merely wanted to read about homesteading, but were not in any danger of actually trying it this year.

 

How was I able to launch a homestead? My homestead did not ultimately work out, because I had the wrong partner. But most of the other ingredients I had down. I think that I had success with getting my act together, to tackle what to many is a daunting task because I put myself through training.

 

Let's look at it this way. Let's suppose that you and I were interested in taking a sixty mile bike ride through the countryside this weekend, and maybe head up into the back country a bit. Would that honestly sound like fun for most of us? Would it even be doable? If you haven't already gone for a couple of twenty mile bike rides this month, then you need to admit to yourself that you're not in shape to do this. Do you have experience dealing with flat tires? I do not. So if this contingency actually happened to us, we suddenly wouldn't be having that much fun at all out there.

 

And the thing to remember, is that a 60 mile bike ride is much easier than a weekend of farm work during harvest season.

 

Here's a better plan. Let's suppose that you and your wife wanted to move out to a farm or a homestead that you all had picked out. Assuming you had already done all of the research, and had already paid it off, you probably next would want to pick the right time a year to head out there. Under ideal circumstances, you would already have enough food, water, tools, medicine, school books, supplies, hardware and timber to last you for three entire years. Let me explain. I will also admit that most of the food you would want to take, probably wouldn't keep for three years anyway so I mean that as a metaphor. Money might suffice in place of food.

 

But assuming that you had all of those supplies, and you had $20k in cash, and you had another $20k in a bailout fund, all that you're really trying to do at that point is just work on getting your farm off of the ground, and then maybe learning one or two new things per year. If you're trying to bootstrap your farm and learn a couple of crafts while undertaking basic survival exercises, you will live in complete misery and probably do a rotten job at the above. You will want to have all of the basics squared away and come in already knowing one or two crafts or trades. Heck, your wife should probably know a couple as well. If you intend to hunt, you will want to have a year to do this and to practice your skills up to a professional level and not to have to worry about paying for ammunition, or even killing something for dinner, for that matter.

 

I would be giving any of the same to someone who were trying to start a business in the city - they'd want to have two years of operating capitol. They should focus on the tasks of getting their first two customers, and then getting their first two accounts, and then growing those accounts to the point where business is coming in by referral, without worrying about having to panhandle for their super while doing this very difficult work.

 

Survivalism can be fun as an art or a hobby, but actual survival situations usually aren't much fun for most participants. Homesteading can make a great lifestyle, business or hobby, but you'll want to walk into it with the right level of supplies, the right skill set and some room for your new business to grow. Expect this to take a couple of years to figure out.
